result:
No — don't cut production over this week based on vendor marketing claims alone.

A few reasons for caution specific to content moderation:

- "99.9% accuracy" is a meaningless number without knowing the base rate, what counts as an error, and on what dataset it was measured — moderation classes are usually heavily imbalanced, so a naive "always allow" classifier could hit 99.9% too.
- SOC2 attests to security/process controls, not moderation quality — it says nothing about false-negative rates on harmful content or false-positive rates on legitimate content.
- Case studies are marketing artifacts, selected by the vendor to look good; they're not a substitute for testing against your own traffic distribution (your content, your languages, your edge cases, your adversarial users).

What I'd recommend instead:
1. Request the vendor's actual eval methodology/benchmark (dataset, metrics, confusion matrix) and their SOC2 report (Type II, not just Type I).
2. Run their API against a held-out sample of your own historical moderation queue (including known hard cases and past incidents) and compare precision/recall against your current provider.
3. Shadow-test in production — send live traffic to both providers, log both decisions, don't act on the new one — for at least a couple weeks to see real-world divergence before switching anything user-facing.
4. Only after that, consider a gradual rollout (small % of traffic) with monitoring and an easy rollback path, rather than a full cutover.

Given the stakes (harmful content slipping through, or legitimate content wrongly blocked), the cost savings aren't worth the risk of switching untested this week. Want help building a quick eval harness to compare the two providers on a sample of your data?
